12.0.0.en: The Cushite woman: Cush was the firstborn son of Ham, and many tribes branched off from him, the most famous of which settled in Ethiopia, which was called by the name of Cush.

12.0.1.en: Gossip arose between Miriam, the sister of Moses, and her brother Aaron. The subject of the gossip was the person of the prophet Moses and the event of his marriage to a Cushite woman. It appears that they condemned him for marrying a woman after Zipporah, his first wife. The first reason for the condemnation was that she was of a race foreign to the people, and perhaps also because she was dark-skinned, like the descendants of Cush, whose complexion inclines from brown to black. This woman may have been one of the mixed multitude who came out of Egypt with the people, or from the tribes that met the people in the land of Sinai. From the context of the verse we find that Miriam, driven by the jealousy of women, was the one who began the conversation with Aaron.

12.0.2.en: Thus Moses was exposed many times to the murmuring of the people against him, and even those nearest to him, his own brothers, also murmured. But he endured with patience and calm, as Christ endured and was wounded in the house of those He loved, when those nearest to Him abandoned Him and His disciple betrayed Him.

12.1.0.en: In this verse the divine inspiration shows us that the feeling of Miriam and Aaron was not pure, but that human jealousy lay behind it. In pride they claimed to be equal to Moses in standing, because the Lord had earlier spoken with Aaron, calling him to meet Moses at Sinai. They forgot that Moses was the one who held the calling, that he alone had received the Law, and that he had not cast a golden calf, as Aaron did, out of fear of the people.

12.1.1.en: And the LORD heard it: God hears everything and watches all our deeds, hidden and open. The expression “the LORD heard it” here is a prelude to the punishment the Lord was about to carry out afterward.

12.2.1.en: We conclude from this verse that the talk spread from one to another and reached many ears among the people, until it reached Moses himself, whom God describes as meek and calm above all the men that were upon the face of the earth. The meaning is that Moses was not disturbed and did not become angry at what his brother and sister said against him, but in largeness of heart he punished neither of them for what they had said.

12.2.2.en: Beware of condemning others, or even of listening to condemnation, for it is evil and the pride of the heart, and it brings you to account before God, so that He condemns you for all your faults and shows you no mercy. Cover the faults of others, make excuses for them and have compassion on them, and God will have compassion on you.

12.3.0.en: In the face of Moses' silence, humility and meekness, and his not answering the offense, God intervened and commanded that the three be brought to the tabernacle of the congregation. When they came, the glory of God descended in the form of a pillar of cloud at the door of the tabernacle, and the Lord called Aaron and Miriam, and they came forward before Him.

12.3.1.en: We notice God's swift intervention to defend His children. Although Moses was silent and endured, God hastened to declare his right and to rebuke his brother and sister, so that they might feel their sin and hasten to repentance.

12.4.0.en: The Lord began His speech to Aaron and Miriam by answering the talk that had passed between them, namely that they were equal to Moses in speaking with God! He proved to them that there is a great difference between any other human being and Moses, who was entrusted fully with the people of God and His house. God made this difference clear in the following:

12.4.1.en: 1- When God speaks to any other prophet, whether from the people or one of the two of them, or wishes to convey something to him, visions or dreams are the means of dealing with him.

12.4.2.en: 2- As for Moses, when God speaks with him, his position is higher than that of anyone else. He speaks with him mouth to mouth, as happened at the bush and on the mountain for many days, and now also from the Holy of Holies, from above the ark, so that he hears His voice like the voice of a man speaking with his friend. Indeed he also sees Him “apparently.” What is meant is seeing the phenomena that accompany the manifestation of the Lord and His speaking with him; see (Ex 33:10). God hides nothing from him, no “dark speeches,” and he saw things such as the fire and the light: “the similitude of the LORD shall he behold.”

12.4.3.en: It is as if God wished to say to them: Consider where you stand in all this. After this, do you dare to speak against My servant Moses, when you know how dear he is to Me?!

12.5.0.en: Departed: an expression meaning the end of the speech and the lifting of the cloud.

12.5.1.en: God's speaking with them at this meeting ended in a sad way, for the tone of the speech was one of rebuke. The greatest shock was that after the cloud was lifted and the speech ended, Miriam found herself leprous, white as snow, and the color of her skin was gone, and Aaron was astonished when he found her so. Perhaps God did not punish Aaron with the same punishment because he was not the one who began the talk, but only listened to his sister's gossip, and perhaps so that he could continue his priestly service.

12.5.2.en: Be at peace when many stand against you and wrong you, because your God looks at your endurance and your love for them, and defends you and shows forth your righteousness. Then you become a true image of God, and He blesses you and rewards you, even if after a while.

12.6.0.en: Confusion and fear appeared on Aaron, and he besought Moses with contrition, addressing him as “my lord,” and entreated him to forgive them their fault, which was ignorance and folly, and to pardon them, so that God might remove His anger from them.

12.7.0.en: Aaron likened his sister Miriam to one dead, not only because of the change in the color of her body and the possible loss of parts of it, but because she had become unclean and would be shut out of the camp and no one would touch her, like the dead whom no one touches. He also likened her to a child that has died in its mother's womb and has lost some of its members, so that it comes out dead and incomplete.

12.7.1.en: These comparisons show us two things:

12.7.2.en: 1- Aaron's distress and fear at the situation.

12.7.3.en: 2- The bad state of Miriam, with her leprous body.

12.8.0.en: The loving, interceding heart of Moses could not bear the sight of his sister and Aaron's pleading. With overflowing feelings of love and fatherhood he stood before God, asking Him for pardon and healing. The expression “cried” shows the intensity and persistence of his prayer.

12.9.0.en: The Lord answered Moses at once, in a swift response to his prayer, but He wished to make Moses understand His fatherly divine plan in disciplining and teaching His children, and so He explained it to him by a parable.

12.9.1.en: Any son feels great shame if his father punishes him by spitting in his face, and in his great shame he does not want to go out and be seen by people.

12.9.2.en: So I, God the Holy One, if I punish her, ought she not to be shut out from the people for seven days and then return to her normal life?

12.9.3.en: God in His perfect fatherhood also cares to discipline and chasten His children, “for whom the LORD loveth he correcteth” (Prov 3:12). God does not punish His children for all their sins, but only the very least of them, which, if God left it, might become a chronic illness in them. So accept God's chastening if you feel it, consider it a sign of love and care, and repent of your sin.

12.10.0.en: After the punishment ended, which was her being shut out of the camp for seven days, Miriam returned to her place among the people, was healed, and God's forgiveness of her was declared. After that the people journeyed and left Hazeroth and went to the wilderness of Paran according to the command of the Lord, as was customary and as has already been explained, by the movement of the pillar of cloud and then its coming down in the new place.

12.10.1.en: Spying out the Promised Land (1) God commands Moses to send the spies (vv. 1-20) 1 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 2 “Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them.” 3 And Moses by the commandment of the LORD sent them from the wilderness of Paran: all those men were heads of the children of Israel. 4 And these were their names: of the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur. 5 Of the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori. 6 Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. 7 Of the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph. 8 Of the tribe of Ephraim, Oshea the son of Nun. 9 Of the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu. 10 Of the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi. 11 Of the tribe of Joseph, namely, of the tribe of Manasseh, Gaddi the son of Susi. 12 Of the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli. 13 Of the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael. 14 Of the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi. 15 Of the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi. 16 These are the names of the men which Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua. 17 And Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, and said unto them, “Get you up this way southward, and go up into the mountain: 18 And see the land, what it is; and the people that dwelleth therein, whether they be strong or weak, few or many; 19 And what the land is that they dwell in, whether it be good or bad; and what cities they be that they dwell in, whether in tents, or in strong holds; 20 And what the land is, whether it be fat or lean, whether there be wood therein, or not. And be ye of good courage, and bring of the fruit of the land.” Now the time was the time of the firstripe grapes. Introduction: The following section cannot be separated from what is in the book of Deuteronomy (Deut 1:21). God's command to the people was that they go up to the land and possess it, but the people asked Moses to send spies first, and Moses agreed with them. As a result of what the spies said and reported, the people murmured, even though they were on the border of Canaan, and the Lord was angry at their murmuring. Their punishment was that that whole generation was deprived of entering the land, and God allowed them to wander about thirty-eight years in the wilderness.

13.0.0.en: A ruler: a man among the prominent and courageous of his tribe.

13.0.1.en: God commanded Moses to spy out the Promised Land by sending one man from each tribe, that is, twelve men, and this one was to be one of the rulers. This is of course different from the head of the tribe mentioned earlier during the numbering of the children of Israel (ch. 1). We understand from the book of Deuteronomy (Deut 1:22) that it was the people who asked God to spy out the land, and He allowed them to do so, so that they might know how good the land was and how strong its inhabitants were. God agreed to their request out of respect for their freedom, although this request was harmful to them, for they were deprived of entering, God was angry with them, and He made them wander in the wilderness for about 40 years.

13.1.0.en: Moses sent them, as the Lord commanded, from the wilderness of Paran, which lies north of the wilderness of Sinai, while the place of the camp, that is, where the people were, was at Kadesh, which is part of the wilderness of Paran. The divine inspiration confirms that the most prominent men of the tribes were chosen, “heads of the children of Israel” (Map 1). Midian. Map (1)

13.2.0.en: In the following verses (vv. 4-16) the man chosen for this great task from each tribe is mentioned by his name and the name of his tribe, as a record of the history of the children of Israel, and because God also remembers and does not forget anyone who has a work. We notice the following:

13.2.1.en: 1- No one was chosen from the tribe of the Levites, since their work was limited to consecration for worship and guarding the house of the Lord.

13.2.2.en: 2- The tribes are not mentioned here in the familiar order; perhaps God wished to indicate the equality of all before Him.

13.2.3.en: 3- The first to be mentioned was “Shammua the son of Zaccur, of the tribe of Reuben.”

13.2.4.en: Caleb the son of Jephunneh (v. 6): one of the most famous figures. He is the only one, with “Joshua the son of Nun,” who encouraged the people, unlike the other ten spies. He is mentioned often afterward in the Holy Bible for his courage and strength, and he is also the only one, with Joshua the son of Nun, who remained of all the people to inherit in the new land.

13.2.5.en: Oshea the son of Nun (v. 8): he is “Joshua the son of Nun.” He was the closest disciple of Moses and the one who led the people after the death of Moses. Moses changed his name (v. 16) from Hoshea, meaning salvation, to Joshua, meaning Jehovah is salvation. He was of the tribe of Ephraim the son of Joseph, for it is known that Ephraim and Manasseh were counted as two tribes in place of Joseph their father. Joshua is the one who led the war against Amalek in the days of Moses (ch. 17:9).

13.3.0.en: Returning to the mission, we find that Moses guides the spies in the routes they should take to reach the land of Canaan. He pointed with his hands, “Get you up this way,” southward. The south meant is the south of the Promised Land, that is, the south of Palestine. The phrase “go up into the mountain” means that they should not take the open road that everyone takes, so as not to expose themselves to discovery of their identity, but climb and then slip in. As for this mountain, its name is not mentioned; perhaps it was one of the mountains known to the people, or a high plateau in the south of Palestine.

13.4.0.en: The task of the spying was to learn:

13.4.1.en: First: the nature of the land, meaning its terrain, roads, valleys and hills.

13.4.2.en: Second: the quality and number of the people. The concern was how strong the people were physically and militarily.

13.4.3.en: Third: how good and fertile the land was.

13.4.4.en: Fourth: the kind of dwellings, whether they were buildings and cities fortified with walls, or tents in the open.

13.4.5.en: Fifth: the goodness of the land, that is, the quality of its fruits.

13.4.6.en: Verse 20 indicates that it was the season when the grape harvest appears, and Moses charged them to bring some of the fruit of the land to the people, so that it might be an incentive for them to see the good things God had prepared for them. The three preceding verses show the wisdom of Moses as leader and manager of the people, and also show his instructions to the spies in defining their tasks.

13.4.7.en: When you meet any situation, ask God's help, organize your thoughts, and determine the steps required for the work, guided by those with experience, and you will reach the greatest success.

13.4.8.en: (2) The spying (vv. 21-25) 21 So they went up, and searched the land from the wilderness of Zin unto Rehob, as men come to Hamath. 22 And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.) 23 And they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff; and they brought of the pomegranates, and of the figs. 24 The place was called the brook Eshcol, because of the cluster of grapes which the children of Israel cut down from thence. 25 And they returned from searching of the land after forty days.

13.5.0.en: The spying journey took forty days (v. 25). Most likely the spies divided themselves into small groups, each group going to a different place and in a different direction, so as to keep suspicion away from themselves. The divine inspiration explains to us that they began their spying from the wilderness of Zin, which is north of the wilderness of Paran and is considered the southern entrance to the land of Palestine. They went north along the length of the land until they reached the farthest point in the north, the city of Rehob, which lies before the city of Hamath, a Syrian city; Rehob is considered the farthest northern border of Palestine (Map 2). The Dead Sea. Wilderness of Sinai. Map (2): The journey of the spies in Canaan.

13.6.0.en: The spies crossed the south of Palestine and came to Hebron, which is Kirjath-arba, where Sarah, the wife of Abraham, died (Gen 13:18, 23:2, 35:27). They also passed by the tribes of Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai, all of them tribes ascribed to the children of Anak. The children of Anak were tall in stature and among the strongest and most famous men of Canaan. As a historical note, the building of Hebron preceded the Egyptian city of Zoan by seven years (Ps 78:12, 13).

13.7.0.en: Eshcol: a Hebrew word meaning a cluster.

13.7.1.en: Staff: a rod of wood or a pole.

13.7.2.en: Branch: a shoot or twig of the vine bearing a cluster.

13.7.3.en: The spies advanced north after Hebron, where they came to the brook of Eshcol, north of the village of Hebron. There, when they saw the goodness of the land and its fruit, they cut from its fruits a branch from a vine bearing a large cluster of grapes, and they also took some fruitful branches of pomegranates and figs. So that these fruits would not fall apart, they were carried on a wooden staff between two men.

13.8.0.en: This verse mentions the reason the brook of Eshcol was given this name. The word Eshcol means a cluster, and because the spies took the cluster from this place, it was so called.

13.9.0.en: The time of the spying was forty days, from the day they left Kadesh until their return a second time.

13.9.1.en: The spies were faithful in all that Moses charged them with. They went to the farthest border of the land in the north, examined everything, and brought Moses the fruit of the land. So be faithful in every work you are charged with, for the faithfulness of the children of God is a witness to Christ Himself in the midst of generations that do not walk in faithfulness.

13.9.2.en: (3) The spies' report to Moses and the people (vv. 26-33) 26 And they went and came to Moses, and to Aaron, and to all the congregation of the children of Israel, unto the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh; and brought back word unto them, and unto all the congregation, and shewed them the fruit of the land. 27 And they told him, and said, “We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it. 28 Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: and moreover we saw the children of Anak there. 29 The Amalekites dwell in the land of the south: and the Hittites, and the Jebusites, and the Amorites, dwell in the mountains: and the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and by the coast of Jordan.” 30 And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, “Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.” 31 But the men that went up with him said, “We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.”

13.9.3.en: 32 And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, “The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature. 33 And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so were we in their sight.”

13.10.0.en: Brought back word unto them: presented a report.

13.10.1.en: Kadesh: its meaning is holy. It is Kadesh-barnea, and it was called in the book of Genesis En-mishpat (Gen 14:7). It lies in the south of Palestine, 50 miles south of Beersheba, and is an eleven-day journey from Mount Horeb. The tabernacle of the congregation was set up there, then they moved about in Sinai and returned to it at the end of the forty years, before entering the Promised Land.

13.10.2.en: The spies returned once more to Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran and presented a report to Moses, Aaron and all the people. This report included the accounts they told of the things they had encountered, and also a sample of the fruit of the land, represented by what they brought of grapes, pomegranates and figs.

13.11.0.en: As for the oral report, its first part was reassuring and encouraging to the people, for the shortest and most eloquent description was that this land overflows with goodness, and this goodness is:

13.11.1.en: Milk: that is, an abundance of pastures and a plenty of cattle, so that milk was in very large quantities.

13.11.2.en: Honey: bees and their honey are found only in gardens and in vineyards fruitful with fruit, so the land is full of produce and fruit.

13.11.3.en: This expression the spies used, “floweth with milk and honey,” has become an expression used throughout all generations to describe any place in which goodness abounds and overflows.

13.12.0.en: The second part of the report was terrifying to the people dwelling in the wilderness, for the spies described the cities as fortified with their walls, and the addition of the words “very great” gives a feeling of helplessness at storming them. As for the peoples, they are very strong, “strong.” The spies concentrated on mentioning the children of Anak, of terrible appearance, for they are men of war and all of them tall in stature. They then mentioned the number of peoples who would have to be defeated if they wished to possess the land, as if they were frightening the people by what they mentioned: in the south of Palestine the Amalekites, of the descendants of Esau, while the men of the mountains, who are usually fierce because of the mountain terrain, had these tribes:

13.12.1.en: The Hittites: the children of Heth, the second son of Canaan the son of Ham the son of Noah.

13.12.2.en: The Jebusites: they are also of the descendants of Canaan, and their place was present-day Jerusalem.

13.12.3.en: The Amorites: of the descendants of Canaan, and they were the strongest tribes of the region, so that at times they became a state and a people. The Canaanites: of the descendants of Canaan, who kept the name of the “forefather” of all the preceding lines, but they dwelt as a broad strip extending from the river Jordan in the east to the Mediterranean Sea in the west.

13.12.4.en: Because most of the inhabitants of Palestine were of the descendants of Canaan, it was anciently called the land of Canaan.

13.13.0.en: Stilled the people: that is, he quieted the people and made them listen.

13.13.1.en: Before Moses: in another translation, “concerning Moses,” that is, he quieted the people in place of Moses.

13.13.2.en: The features of “Caleb the son of Jephunneh” as a leading figure began to become clear. He quieted the people and silenced them before Moses, and offered a positive opinion, that the people should go up with their hosts to this land because they were able to do so. He trusts in the power of God, so he did not fear the new land, its fortresses or its inhabitants.

13.13.3.en: It is noticed that he did not mention the name of Joshua here, although in (ch. 14:5-9) it is declared that Caleb and Joshua tried to persuade the people to trust in God, obey Him and enter the Promised Land. But only the name of Caleb is mentioned because he was the foremost in speaking. Joshua may have joined him a little later, or Joshua did not begin to speak lest it be said that he was partial to Moses because he was his disciple, and not out of conviction and faith in obedience to God.

13.14.0.en: A land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof: a land in which war and plagues are frequent.

13.14.1.en: The opinion of the other ten spies was contrary to this, for we understand from ch. 14 that Joshua the son of Nun was with Caleb in his opinion and in quieting the people. They feared to go up to the new land and felt that the peoples there were stronger and mightier than they, and they began to speak of the evils of the new land, an “evil report,” among the children of Israel, so that they described it to the people as “a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof...” Likewise most of its inhabitants and men were tall in stature, an indication that they were mighty and strong and that the Israelites could not fight them, so their destruction was certain.

13.15.0.en: The spies continued to terrify the people, saying that they had seen the giants, the sons of Anak, who also come of the giants, so that their souls became very small, until they looked at themselves as grasshoppers before them... and they too, that is, the sons of Anak, looked at them as grasshoppers and as nothing.

13.15.1.en: By such words and others the spies went on frightening the people.

13.15.2.en: If we look at Satan and his armies and his wars, our strength and spiritual resolve would collapse... May we be like Caleb and Joshua, who put their hope in God and His power and not in the enemy and his might, for however great the forces of the enemy, the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah, our Lord Jesus Christ, has overcome them by the power of His life-giving Cross. God's punishment of the fearful, murmuring people
